1:
The long duel of the three friends with Job runs out at last, and the narrator pauses to explain both the silence that has fallen and the young man about to break it. The reformed John Gill reads the opening clause as a weary truce: the three men — Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar — ceased to answer because they grew tired of a contest that was all to no purpose, resting, as the word suggests, as men do on a sabbath, and leaving the way clear for another disputant. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry catches the irony of the arrangement, that usually young men dispute and old men moderate, but here, as a rebuke to the elders' unbecoming heat, a young man is raised up to moderate; and he doubts the friends' stated reason, for they said they ceased because Job was 'righteous in his own eyes,' whereas he was really righteous before God, so that they made this the excuse only to save their own credit when they found themselves run aground.

The grammatical-historical witnesses set the scene with their usual care. Keil and Delitzsch note that this historical introduction, though prose, is pointed in the poetical accentuation, since a change of mode in so small a compass would have seemed awkward; and they read the friends' silence as their exhaustion, so that Job seems to have come off the conqueror. Charles Ellicott dwells on the newcomer's pedigree — Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the kindred of Ram — tracing Buz to the son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, in Genesis 22:21, and finding in the very specification of his lineage a mark that he was a real and not an imaginary personage.

Over the phrase 'righteous in his own eyes' a genuine textual difference opens. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reports that the Septuagint, Syriac, Arabic, and Chaldee, supported by a thirteenth-century manuscript of Kennicott's, all read 'righteous in their eyes,' intimating that the friends were now convinced Job was a holy man and had charged him foolishly, a reading Symmachus echoes with 'because he appeared more righteous than themselves.' Gill, Henry, and Ellicott keep the received text, that Job was righteous 'in his own eyes.' Beneath these voices stands the oldest, the latin-fathers Gregory the Great, who frames the whole section that opens here: through the next chapters, while Job keeps silence, Elihu, a younger person, enters upon many right and sound topics, yet not rightly, nor with a sound intention — a verdict on the new speaker that the rest of the chapter will spend itself debating.
2:
The narrator names the young man's anger and its first cause, that Elihu's wrath was kindled against Job 'because he justified himself rather than God.' The reformed John Gill pauses over the identity of this new figure, dismissing the traditions that would either debase him as Balaam the soothsayer — whom neither his date nor his character fits — or exalt him as the Messiah, since Elihu speaks of the coming One as another than himself. For though the very names might be strained toward the Messiah — Elihu, 'my God is he'; Barachel, 'the son of the blessed God'; of the kindred of Ram, the high and holy line; the Buzite, one despised and reproached — there are other things in the speeches that cannot be said of Christ at all, so that Elihu is rather a holy and good man whose whole discourse shows it. The wesleyan-arminian voices weigh both the anger and the pedigree. Adam Clarke insists the kindled wrath means no more than that Elihu was greatly excited and zealous to vindicate the justice and providence of God, and, tracing Buz to the second son of Nahor and Ram to Aram the son of Kemuel, reads the charge literally — Elihu felt that Job 'justified his soul,' naphsho, defending not only his conduct but his very motives, before God. John Wesley marks that the pedigree is set down partly for Elihu's honour, as a wise and good man, and chiefly to evidence the truth of the history, and unfolds the name: Elihu signifies 'my God is he' — they had all tried in vain to convince Job, but 'my God is he who both can and will do it.'

The grammatical-historical witnesses fix the wording and the fault. Keil and Delitzsch render that Elihu's wrath burned against Job because he justified himself at the expense of God, and against the three friends because they had found no answer and yet had condemned him. Charles Ellicott points the reader back to Job 19:6, where Job's maintaining of his innocence could not, in his own mind, be reconciled with the justice of God; yet Ellicott is careful to hold the balance, recalling that the same Job had declared God to be his salvation in Job 13:16, and had owned that no man can be absolutely just with God. The charge, then, is not that Job was wicked but that in his pain he had grown more anxious to clear his own name than to clear God's; and on that single point, the witnesses agree, the young man's indignation fastens.
3:
The second ground of Elihu's anger falls on the friends, and the witnesses read it as the mark of a would-be moderator who will spare neither side. The reformed John Gill observes that Elihu took part with neither Job nor his accusers but blamed both, and that what most displeased him in the three was their double failure — they had found no answer to Job's arguments, and yet they had condemned him all the same. The wesleyan-arminian voices sharpen the contradiction. Adam Clarke puts it plainly: they had condemned Job, and yet could not answer his reasonings on the general subject or in vindication of himself; the sentence stood without the proof that alone could warrant it. John Wesley reads the same fault in two strokes — they had made no answer to Job's arguments as to the main cause, and had nonetheless condemned him as a bad man.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott states the injustice in its barest form: the friends could not reply unto Job, nor deny that he had been in conduct such as he claimed, and yet they concluded that he must be wicked because God had smitten him — reasoning backward from his affliction to a guilt they could not otherwise establish. It is precisely this that a fair mind cannot bear, that men should hold fast a verdict whose premises they have failed to make good; and Elihu, the witnesses agree, is angry not as a partisan but as one offended by unfairness itself.

Henry's portrait of the young moderator hovers over the verse. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, taking part with neither, judges Elihu equally displeased with the mistakes and mismanagement of both, for seldom is a quarrel begun, and more seldom carried on so far, in which there is not a fault on both sides. Those who in good earnest seek for truth must be impartial toward the contenders, neither rejecting what is true and good on either side for the sake of what is amiss, nor defending what is amiss for the sake of what is good, but learning to separate between the precious and the vile. So the verse completes the double indictment: Job had wronged God's honour, and the friends had wronged their brother; and the anger kindled at both is, in the witnesses' reading, the anger of a man who cares more for the truth of the case than for the standing of either party to it.
4:
Before the young man speaks, the narrator accounts for his long forbearance: he 'had waited till Job had spoken,' holding back because his elders had the right of first speech. The reformed John Gill takes the clause simply, that Elihu waited until Job had made an end — 'the words of Job are ended' — and until the three friends too had said all they had to say. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the grammar of the delay: he had waited for Job 'with words,' that is, until Job should have spoken his last word in the controversy, the perfect standing for the pluperfect; and he deferred because the three 'were older than he in days,' so that seniority, not any inferiority of understanding, kept him silent.

Charles Ellicott makes this the place to lay out the whole line Elihu will take, an intermediate one, neither Job's nor the friends'. He admits, or at least does not deny, the integrity of Job, though he uses very strong expressions about the course Job has adopted; but he holds that the divine afflictions have a disciplinary object, and may be sent because God has discerned in the sufferer the seeds of unfaithfulness and defection — a purpose that may explain their meaning even in Job's case. Elihu has, Ellicott notes, very lofty ideas of the righteousness of God and of his power and majesty; he holds that the Almighty cannot be found out, yet that his mercy and justice may be safely trusted, and it is to this position that he will lead Job before the Lord answers out of the whirlwind.

The verse also opens Henry's meditation on the decorum of the scene. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry commends the modesty by which Elihu waited on Job's speeches until they were ended, and on the friends' silence, not because they were wiser but because they were older, unwilling to abridge them of the privilege that seniority claims. Some rules of precedency must be observed for the keeping of order; and the young may the better pay such respect because they shall receive it when they come to be seniors. So the delay is no accident but a courtesy, and the witnesses read in it the temper of the speaker — patient, deferential, and yet, as the kindled wrath has shown, resolved at last to say what the elders had left unsaid.
5:
The last line of the prose frame gathers up the friends' defeat and the kindling it provoked: when Elihu 'saw that there was no answer in the mouth of these three men,' his wrath was kindled. The reformed John Gill weighs the emptiness of that silence — there was no answer that could be called an answer; the three, men of years and experience and reputed wise and knowing, were quite nonplussed and put to silence, and it was the spectacle of so helpless a muteness in the aged that stirred the young man at last to speak. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark that the Elihu section has in part a peculiar vocabulary of its own, and dwell on the rare verb behind his opening confession — a word cognate with the Arabic for drawing back or retreating in fear, so that when he says he 'stood back and was afraid' the very term pictures a man who had kept himself on one side and held his knowledge in.

With this the introduction closes and the speech proper is about to begin, and the witnesses feel the hinge. Elihu had waited on the elders out of deference; now that their store is spent and their mouths are stopped, the deference has nothing left to wait for, and the silence that fell at v.1 becomes the very ground of his warrant to speak. The order of the scene is not lost on the witnesses: he does not thrust himself in while the elders still hold the floor, but waits until their failure is complete, so that his speaking is a filling of the void they leave, not a breaking-in upon a turn that is not his.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the whole approach as a study in a diffidence that is not cowardice. Elihu was a man of great modesty and humility, who, though young and able, was not pert or confident or assuming; his face shone, and, like Moses, he did not know it. He had applied his mind so closely to all that passed that he had formed a judgment of it, yet was slow to deliver that judgment because he differed from men older than himself. It becomes us, Henry draws from it, to be suspicious of our own judgment in matters of doubtful disputation, swift to hear the sentiments of others and slow to speak our own, especially when we go against those whose learning and piety we justly venerate. So the frame ends where the speech will begin — with a young man who has watched and weighed and waited, and whose long silence has earned him the right to be heard.
6:
At last the young man opens his mouth, and his first word is an apology for his years: 'I am young, and ye are very old; wherefore I was afraid, and durst not shew you mine opinion.' The reformed John Gill notes that since there was no answer left in the elders, Elihu takes it upon himself to give one, but first makes an apology on account of his youth. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the confession 'I am young in days, and ye are hoary,' and hear in it the peculiar diction of this section — 'therefore I stood back and was afraid to show you my knowledge.' The wesleyan-arminian voices set the manners of the East behind the words: Adam Clarke observes that among the Asiatics the young never spoke in the presence of their elders, above all on a subject of controversy, so that Elihu's hesitation is not affectation but custom; John Wesley glosses the fear simply as the dread of being thought forward and presumptuous. Charles Ellicott finds the whole manner of Elihu's coming forward 'very interesting, and full of character,' giving a picture of the times and habits of the age.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the verse a model for the young. Here is a man of abilities who was yet not confident or assuming, but had so diffident a sense of his own judgment that, how clear soever the matter was to him, he was afraid to deliver his mind because he differed from those older than he. It becomes us, Henry urges, to be suspicious of our own judgment in matters of doubtful disputation, swift to hear the sentiments of others and slow to speak our own, especially when we go contrary to the judgment of those whom, for their learning and piety, we justly reverence. Yet the modesty is not the whole of him: Henry sees in Elihu a man who also knew when and how to speak as well as when to keep silence, one who had so much respect to his friends as not to interrupt them, and yet so much regard to truth and justice — his better friends — as not to betray them by his silence.

So the opening word is at once a bow and a challenge. Elihu owns his youth and the deference it owes; but the very care with which he has waited, listened, and weighed makes the coming claim the weightier, for a judgment so slow to speak is not likely to prove rash when at last it does.
7:
Elihu recalls the maxim that had held him back: 'I said, Days should speak, and multitude of years should teach wisdom.' The reformed John Gill unfolds the phrase as meaning men of days, men who have lived many days and years; to such it belongs to speak, and their place should not be usurped, for from length of years one might reasonably expect instruction that is to the purpose and to edification. It is the elders' place and their duty, Gill allows, to speak and to instruct their juniors and all who are under them, and from men of many days one might justly look for profit when at last they open their mouths. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet 'Let age speak, and the multitude of years teach wisdom,' and set it as the opinion Elihu had held until a deeper consideration overturned it in the verse following. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills in the cultural ground: men were reputed wise and experienced in proportion to the years they had lived, and the boasted wisdom of the East consisted largely in proverbs and maxims treasured up on every subject, so that the aged were the natural keepers of that store.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs both the truth of the maxim and its limits. Age and experience do give a man great advantage in judging of things, both furnishing him with more matter for his thoughts to work upon and ripening the faculties he works with; and this is a good reason why old people should take pains to learn and to teach, else the advantages of their age are a reproach to them, and why young people should attend upon their instructions. Henry commends the deference Elihu paid his seniors and the high expectation he had of them, waiting for their words as one who looked to receive much. It is a good lodging, Henry says with the apostle, to be with an old disciple, and young people do well to attend upon the instruction of the aged, whose years should have ripened both their store of matter and the judgment that handles it.

Yet the verse is plainly a concession about to be qualified, and the witnesses feel the 'I said' as a past persuasion rather than a present verdict. Elihu had assumed that wisdom would flow from years; he is on the point of confessing that it does not always do so, and that a higher source than age must be reckoned with. The maxim is honoured — days should speak, and the aged should teach — but it is honoured only to be corrected, and the correction is the burden of all that follows.
8:
'But there is a spirit in man: and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth them understanding' — with this truth Elihu overturns the maxim just honoured, and here the witnesses find the theological heart of his whole apology; and here too they divide over what the 'spirit' is. The reformed John Gill takes it first as a correction of Elihu's former sentiment: since there is a spirit in men, young and old alike, and with it a capacity to teach wisdom not tied to age, he was emboldened to speak. Gill allows that many understand the rational soul, immaterial and immortal, which is in every man and by which he knows, reasons, and judges, and thinks Elihu, conscious of such a spirit in himself, was thereby stirred to enter the debate.

The wesleyan-arminian and grammatical-historical witnesses press rather the divine source. Adam Clarke reads it as an afflatus in mankind: the spirit is in man as the spring of his very existence, and by the breath of the Almighty he is made capable of understanding and of discerning divine truth, an allusion to the breathing of life into man at Genesis 2:7. That same Spirit, Clarke adds, is the true light that lighteth every man in John 1:9, and bears witness with our spirit in Romans 8:16, so that in this one saying Elihu spoke more sound doctrine than the friends had uttered in the whole controversy. Charles Ellicott renders it 'it is the spirit in man, and the breath of the Almighty, that giveth them understanding,' the very language of the Mosaic narrative, and takes Elihu to mean that not years so much as the spirit and illumination of the Almighty make a man pre-eminent in wisdom. John Wesley reduces it to a sentence: the spirit is the Spirit of God, and he gives understanding to whom he pleases. Keil and Delitzsch, keeping the parallelism synonymous, ground man's very life in the Spirit of God, the breath of the Almighty being the principle of that understanding which age of itself cannot confer.

So the debate is real but not bitter: whether the 'spirit' names the rational soul native to every man, as Gill first takes it, or the inbreathed Spirit of the Almighty who gives wisdom where he will, as Clarke, Ellicott, Wesley, and Keil and Delitzsch insist. Either way the argument stands, and it is a levelling one: since understanding is a gift and not a possession of the aged, a young man may have it and the old may lack it, and the verdict must go to the truth and not to the years.
9:
'Great men are not always wise, neither do the aged understand judgment' — the blunt corollary follows at once. The reformed John Gill ranges the senses of 'great' — the great in dignity and rank, the rich and honourable; or the great in number, the multitude, not to be followed merely for being many; or the great in years, well stricken in age; or the great as teachers and masters in Israel. Such men may be wise in natural, civil, and worldly things, and yet not wise in the divine and spiritual, and least of all in the reasons of God's providential dealings, his afflicting of the righteous and sparing of the wicked. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke owns the saying as one that every age and country verifies, and applies it to the case in hand: the aged here did not understand judgment; they had a great many wise and good sayings collected, but showed neither wisdom nor discretion in applying them. John Wesley glosses 'judgment' as what is just and right — the very thing the elders had failed to discern in Job's case.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott takes 'great men' to mean old men, matching Elihu's calling himself little in days, or else the great in the sense of number, the many; and he sets the line beside Job's own tart word to the friends in Job 12:2, 'no doubt but ye are the people, and wisdom shall die with you.' Keil and Delitzsch read the couplet as of a piece with the argument, that the great in years are not therefore wise, nor do the aged of themselves understand what is right.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the practical moral. It is a pity great men are not always wise, for then they would never do hurt with their greatness and would do so much the more good with their wisdom; men should be preferred for wisdom, and those in honour and power have most need of it and the best opportunity of improving in it, yet it does not follow that they have it, and therefore it is folly to subscribe to the dictates of any with an implicit faith. Even the aged may be mistaken, Henry adds, and must not take it as an affront to be contradicted, but rather as a kindness to be instructed by their juniors, for a poor and wise child is better than an old and foolish king.
10:
The two preceding truths — that understanding is God's gift and that greatness is no guarantee of wisdom — give Elihu his warrant, and he draws it out: 'Therefore I said, Hearken to me; I also will shew mine opinion.' The reformed John Gill observes that the address is singular in the Hebrew, spoken to Job and to each of the friends in turn: though Elihu is but a young man, if he has the Spirit of God and the inspiration of the Almighty in him, he may be able to say something worth their hearing. The claim is modest in form and bold in substance — not that his years entitle him, but that the spirit within him may. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the tense, reading 'Therefore I said' as equivalent to 'Therefore I say' — it is what Elihu now concludes, the present resolve that has ripened out of his former convictions.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the force of the 'therefore.' Since the soul is a spirit, capable of receiving and discerning truth, and since this understanding spirit is in every man as the inspiration of the Almighty, one man has reason as well as another, and no man may pretend to engross all the trade of it. Elihu means much what Job had meant in claiming understanding for himself: he does not boast a revelation the elders lack, only a share in the reason that is every man's honour, and from that common endowment he presses his inference — therefore hearken to me. We must be willing, Henry adds, to hear reason even from those every way inferior to us, and to yield to it; for a man of good sight can see further on level ground than a purblind man from the top of a mountain.

So the verse turns the young man's diffidence into a plea. He does not demand a hearing on the ground of age, which he lacks, nor of office, which he does not claim, but on the ground that God gives understanding where he will; and having set that foundation, he asks, for the first time openly, to be heard. It is the request of a man who has earned it by silence: he had waited on their words, weighed their reasons, and found them wanting, and now claims no more than the liberty every reasonable creature may claim, to speak his mind in turn and have it fairly weighed.
11:
Elihu turns from his warrant to his credentials as a listener, protesting in the words 'I waited for your words; I gave ear to your reasons, whilst ye searched out what to say' how patiently he had attended before presuming to speak. The reformed John Gill hears in the waiting a real eagerness — Elihu waited for their words with desire, as a man waits for the rain and the latter rain, in hope of arguments that would fully satisfy and convince; and he waited patiently until they had wholly done — not breaking in, but giving their argument every chance to ripen into something that might satisfy. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke notes a small textual variant, that several of Kennicott's and De Rossi's manuscripts read 'your arguments' where the received text has 'your reasons,' with little change of sense; and he catches the sting in the last clause. 'Whilst ye searched out words' is a fine irony — a picture of the elders casting about, hunting up and down for something to say, which they must have felt as the barb it was.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the patient hearing itself an argument. Elihu waited for their words as one who expected much from them, agreeably to the high opinion he had of grave men; he gave ear to their reasons, that he might take their meaning and fully understand the drift and force of their discourse. And this he did, Henry notes, though they were slow and took up much time in searching out what to say, pausing and hesitating and unready at their work; he overlooked all that, and attended to their reasons, which, if really convincing, he would not think the less so for the poorness of the delivery. This attendance Henry reads as that which both entitled Elihu to speak in his turn and enabled him to judge what had been said: those who have heard may speak, and those who have learned may teach. We must often be willing, Henry adds, to hear what we do not like, else we can never prove all things; and he sets over the whole the old courtesy of debate — hanc veniam petimusque damusque vicissim, this liberty we mutually allow and ask — so that the patience Elihu had shown the elders is the very patience he may now fairly require of them in return.

So the verse is a courtesy that doubles as a claim. By owning how long and how carefully he listened, Elihu establishes that his coming verdict is not the impatience of youth but the ripened judgment of a man who gave the elders every chance to persuade him, and was not persuaded.
12:
The patient listening reaches its verdict, and it is a damning one for the elders: 'I attended unto you, and, behold, there was none of you that convinced Job, or that answered his words.' The reformed John Gill marks the closeness of the attention — Elihu attended with great application, striving as it were to get within them and thoroughly understand their meaning — the better to be sure of the failure he now reports. He had, as it were, got within them, taken the full measure of their meaning, so that when he pronounces them beaten it is not the verdict of a careless listener but of one who had followed every turn of their reasoning. The wesleyan-arminian voices press that failure home. Adam Clarke, noting a reading that would give 'your testimonies' for 'unto you,' insists that though they spoke multitudes of words, there was none of them that confuted Job or overthrew his arguments; John Wesley glosses 'convinced' as convinced by solid and satisfactory answers — the one thing none of them had produced.

The grammatical-historical witnesses agree and sharpen. Charles Ellicott judges that in Elihu's estimate no one had so much as touched the main point of the argument with Job. Keil and Delitzsch render 'there was no one who refuted Job, who answered his sentences, from you,' and note the rapid, emotional force of the passage, the clauses set side by side without connectives, as a speaker in earnest will heap them; the very syntax hurries with the indignation of a man who has listened long and found nothing. The heaping of clause on clause, they suggest, is the mark of a feeling that has outrun the leisurely connectives of calm speech.

Henry reads the same conclusion as the ground of Elihu's right to speak. Having heard them out and observed exactly what they aimed at, the puritan-evangelical commentator says, Elihu knew what to say to it; we should be thoroughly apprised of the sentiments of our brethren before we censure them, for he that answers a matter before he hears it, or having heard it only by halves, it is folly and shame to him, and bespeaks him both impertinent and imperious. Elihu had committed no such folly: he had heard the whole, and the whole had failed. So the verse fixes the failure precisely — not that the friends said too little, but that with all their words they never met Job's case; and it is into that unfilled gap that the young man now steps.
13:
Elihu names the very error he means to forestall in the words 'Lest ye should say, We have found out wisdom: God thrusteth him down, not man' — the complacency of men who mistake their opponent's silence for their own victory. The reformed John Gill reads it as a caution against their being wise in their own conceits: they had not convinced Job, only condemned him, and Elihu will not have them attribute to their own skill a conquest they never won, for all true wisdom is of God and not found out by men. The wesleyan-arminian voices unfold the boast Elihu dreads. Adam Clarke has the friends congratulating themselves that by dint of their own understanding they had found out the true system of God's providence and accounted for all Job's sufferings; had they been able to confute him they would have triumphed in their own self-sufficiency. And the second clause — 'God thrusteth him down, not man' — Clarke reads as their conclusion: this is no accidental calamity but the just judgment of God, and therefore Job must be the wicked man they supposed. John Wesley turns it into providence: God left the friends to their own weakness lest they should ascribe the silencing of Job to their own wisdom, and he presents the maxim as their argument, which, he says in Elihu's person, does not satisfy him, and therefore they must bear with him if he seeks for a better.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott states it compactly: Elihu resolved to speak lest they should think themselves wise and suppose that God was afflicting Job on account of his sins, as though the divine hand in the trouble settled the man's guilt.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the verse a case for speaking when error is dressed as piety. Elihu must speak, lest the friends think their argument against Job conclusive and irrefragable — that his extraordinary afflictions prove God his enemy and himself therefore a wicked man. It is time to speak, Henry says, when we hear errors advanced and disputed for, especially under pretence of supporting the cause of God; when God's judgments are vouched to patronize men's pride and their uncharitable censures of their brethren, then we must speak on God's behalf. Or the boast may run the other way, Henry allows: lest the friends should think they had found out the wisest course — to reason with Job no more, but leave it to God to thrust him down — a resignation that would abandon the sufferer to his misery under colour of piety. So the verse both exposes the friends' false hypothesis and justifies the young man's refusal to let it stand as the last word.
14:
Elihu marks the advantage of his own position: he comes to the dispute cool and unprovoked. 'Now he hath not directed his words against me: neither will I answer him with your speeches.' The reformed John Gill observes that Job had not levelled his arguments against Elihu nor set his words in battle array against him, had not lashed and irritated him as he had the three; and so the young man enters the debate calm and unprovoked, with nothing in view but truth, the glory of God, and the good of Job, and may therefore hope for better success than they had. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke says the same from the other side: 'I am no party in this controversy; he has not spoken a word against me, therefore I have no cause of irritation; I shall speak for truth, not for conquest or revenge.' And Clarke will not answer Job with the friends' speeches, for their passions had been inflamed by contradiction and they had spoken foolishly with their lips. His own speech, he promises, shall carry neither their heat nor their partiality.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the double resolve. Elihu will not reply to Job's protestations of his integrity, but allows the truth of them, and so does not appear as Job's enemy: 'He hath not directed his words against me; I have nothing to say against the main scope of his discourse, nor do I differ from his principles — only a gentle reproof to give him for his passionate expressions.' Neither will he repeat the friends' arguments or go on their principles: 'I will not answer him with your speeches, not with the same matter, for should I only say what has been said I might justly be silenced as impertinent, nor in the same manner; I will not be guilty of that peevishness toward him which I dislike in you.' A controversy already fully handled a wise man will let alone, Henry adds, unless he can amend and improve it; why should he do over again what has been done already? Why, Henry asks with the proverb, should a man actum agere, do the thing that is already done? The wise course is to leave a threshed-out controversy alone unless one can carry it further; and Elihu, believing he can, means neither to prosecute Job with fresh accusation nor to weary the company with the friends' stale matter.

So the verse stakes out fresh ground. Elihu will neither prosecute Job as an enemy nor echo the friends as an ally, but come at the case from a new quarter, unentangled in the heat that had spoiled the debate on both sides.
15:
'They were amazed, they answered no more: they left off speaking' — the scene shifts for a moment to the dumbstruck elders, whose speech has utterly failed. The reformed John Gill reads them as men thunderstruck, quite surprised and astonished to hear a young man talk after this manner. They were astonished, Gill implies, both that one so young should presume to speak at all, and that they themselves, for all their years, had been left with nothing to say. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke records Mr. Good's rendering, that their speeches are dissipated, flirted away, scattered into thin air as words without point or sense; but Clarke himself prefers to take it of Job's friends, who had held their several parts as long as they could hope to keep their ground, and at last, weary of their own repetitions and able to bring nothing new, gave up the contest. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott would give the force better with the present tense — 'they are amazed, they answer no more; they have not a word to say' — the picture of a silence that is not a pause but a defeat.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds in the verse the first of three things that apologize for Elihu's interposing: the stage was clear, and he broke in upon none of the managers on either side. They stood still and answered no more, not only leaving off themselves but waiting to hear if any of the company would speak, so that he had room and fair play given him. They seemed, Henry notes, not fully satisfied with what they had said, else they would have adjourned the court and not stood still expecting what might further be offered. He even allows the pleasant conjecture that Elihu here shows himself the penman of the book, writing as an historian of the very scene — how the elders, surprised at the admirable mixture of boldness and modesty in his preface, left off their whispering and stood still to hear what he would say. They did not gainsay the liberty of speech he desired, Henry notes, but yielded him the floor, surprised into stillness by the mixture of boldness and modesty in his opening.

So the verse clears the ground. The debate has exhausted itself; the old men have nothing left; and into a silence that is itself a confession the young man may lawfully speak, not interrupting them but succeeding them. The silence, in the witnesses' reading, is no mere lull but the visible end of the friends' resources, and it is that very emptiness which gives Elihu his room.
16:
Elihu returns to his own waiting, and to the moment it ended: 'When I had waited — for they spake not, but stood still, and answered no more — I said, I will answer also my part.' The reformed John Gill takes it as the plain sequence: Elihu had waited to observe whether they would make any reply to what he had said, or raise any objection to his engaging in the controversy, and finding none, went on. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke says the same: 'I waited to hear if they had anything to reply to Job; and when I found them in effect speechless, then I ventured to come forward.' The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that some would read the clause as a question — 'and shall I wait because they speak not?' — but that in any case they stand still and make no further reply.

Keil and Delitzsch, taking the verse as the opening of the long declaration that runs to the chapter's end, watch the young speaker gather himself for so much promising. He has a rich store of words for replying, they observe, and dwell on the peculiar defective spellings of this section, the forms of the Elihu speeches marking them off, in small points of language, from the rest of the book. The very spelling of his words, defective where the fuller forms might stand, betrays a hand or an age a little apart, so that the grammarians read these speeches as a distinct layer even in their orthography. The waiting is over; the courtesy that held him silent has run its course; and the emphatic doubling of the 'I also,' 'even I,' shows a man stepping forward in his own right at last.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears beneath the sentence the pressure that will burst out in the verses following: Elihu was uneasy, even in pain, to be delivered of his thoughts, and could forbear no longer — while he was musing the fire burned, shut up in his bones, as the prophet Jeremiah felt the word he could not hold in; and so the enforced silence of respect had become a kind of pain, from which the elders' failure now at last releases him. The waiting, in other words, had cost him something; he had held his peace out of respect, but the matter within him was straining for release, and now that the elders are silent there is nothing left to hold it. So the verse is the pivot of the chapter: the last of the waiting, and the threshold of the speech.
17:
The resolve of the previous verse is now stated for its own sake, doubled for emphasis: 'I will answer also my part, I also will shew mine opinion.' The reformed John Gill takes it simply as Elihu's determination to take his turn in giving an answer to Job, since what the friends had offered was quite insufficient and unsuitable to the case. He would take his turn, Gill says, and give the answer they had failed to give, not to silence Job but to meet him where they could not. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fastens on the Hebrew, aaneh chelki, 'I will recite my portion,' and draws from it his standing view of the book: that Job is a sort of drama in which several persons have their several parts to recite, and was perhaps used so in ancient times for public instruction. Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar had each recited their parts, and Job had responded to each, yet nothing was brought to an issue; Elihu, a bystander who had perceived this, now comes forward to take a part, when all the rest had spent their materials — though even he, Clarke adds, would prove unable to close the controversy, which God himself must at last decide. The picture Clarke draws is of a set piece rehearsed in turn: each disputant with his portion to recite, the exchange running its course without resolution, until a fresh voice, unbidden and unassigned, steps from among the listeners to speak a part of his own.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the modesty that still tempers the boldness. Elihu does not pretend to give a definitive sentence; the judgment is the Lord's, and by him it must be determined who is in the right and who in the wrong. But since each of them has shown his opinion, Elihu also will show his, and let it take its fate with the rest. When what is offered, even by the meanest, is offered thus modestly, Henry says, it is a pity but it should be fairly heard and considered. There is no arrogance in it, Henry insists: Elihu does not set himself up as arbiter, but only asks the same fair hearing the others had, submitting his portion, like theirs, to the one Judge who alone can determine the cause.

So the verse holds the two notes of the whole preface together. Elihu claims his portion — he will answer, he will show his mind — and yet claims it as a portion only, one voice among others submitted to a Judge above them all, not the last word but a word that deserves its hearing.
18:
Elihu accounts for his eagerness by the pressure of a mind too full to keep still: 'For I am full of matter, the spirit within me constraineth me.' The reformed John Gill is careful that this is no mere loquacity: Elihu was not a talkative man, full of empty words, but full of matter, of words that had fulness of substance in them, to the purpose, containing strong reasoning and solid argument; his mind was so charged with them that he could not be easy until he had uttered them. Gill likens him to an able minister of the word, full of the wholesome words of Christ, in whom the word dwells richly, a rich treasure in an earthen vessel. Such fulness, Gill implies, is the very opposite of the fool's, whose abundance of words covers a poverty of sense. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads 'matter' as millim, words or wise sayings, ancient opinions; and hears in the second clause an echo of St. Paul, 'the love of Christ constraineth us,' Elihu reckoning himself under the influence of that Spirit which gives understanding, and anxiously concerned for the welfare of both Job and his friends.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet 'I am full of words; the spirit of my inner nature constraineth me,' noting again the defective spelling that marks the diction of the section, and reading the 'spirit of the inner nature' as the pressure of a conviction that will not be held in. Henry too, the puritan-evangelical voice, hears a man with a great deal to say: full of matter, having carefully attended to all that had been said and made his own reflections on it; and he draws the comfort that when aged men are drawn dry and have spent their stock in discoursing of Providence, God can raise up others, even young men, and fill them with matter for the edifying of his church, for the subject can never be exhausted, though those who speak on it may. The fulness, Henry adds, is a stewardship: a man so charged with good matter is bound to lay it out for others, and to stifle it would be to bury a talent that was given to be used.

So the verse gives the inward reason for the outward boldness. It is not vanity that drives Elihu but fulness — a charge of matter, pressed by a spirit within, that must find vent; and the witnesses, reading him kindly, take the constraint as the mark not of a proud talker but of a man with something true and weighty he cannot in conscience withhold.
19:
'Behold, my belly is as wine which hath no vent; it is ready to burst like new bottles' — the pressure within finds its most vivid figure, the ferment of new wine straining a closed skin. The reformed John Gill explains the image with Ben Gersom, that the belly is as a bottle of wine stopped close, the wine within it new and therefore apt to ferment, needing vent given it. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills in the whole picture from the life of the East. The wine is new, in a state of effervescence; the 'bottles' are not glass but bags made of goat-skins, the animal cased whole out of its hide, the skin dressed and the openings tied, with an aperture left for pouring in and drawing out. Clarke has one such skin before him as he writes, well tanned and ornamented, able to hold many gallons, and serving, he notes, not only for wine and water but for butter and various dry goods; and he explains that when the wine ferments and the skin has no vent, the bag is ready to burst, and if it be old the new wine breaks the old stitching or rends the worn skin — the very figure our Lord uses of new wine and old bottles in Matthew 9:17. Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, glosses 'new bottles' simply as wine-skins, and points to the same word of Christ.

Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet 'my interior is like wine which is not opened, like new bottles it is ready to burst,' keeping the ferment and the strain of a vessel that must give way. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers up the force of the image: never did nurse, when her breasts were gorged, so long to have them drawn as Elihu longed to deliver his mind concerning Job's case; had any of the disputants hit the right joint he would contentedly have been silent, but thinking they all missed it, he was eager to be trying his hand. The comparison, homely as it is, measures the intensity of the man's longing: not a wish to be heard, but a need, like the body's need to be relieved of what painfully distends it.

So the verse turns the abstract 'constraint' of the last into something the reader can feel: a swelling, working fulness that must either find an outlet or do violence to the man who holds it in. The young speaker is not merely willing to talk; he is, by his own account, on the very point of bursting to be heard.
20:
The straining skin must be opened, and Elihu names the relief that speaking will bring: 'I will speak, that I may be refreshed: I will open my lips and answer.' The reformed John Gill hears a man determined to disburden himself: the matter he was full of lay with weight upon him, pressed him hard, and gave him pain, and therefore he resolves to speak his mind and be eased. Gill draws the minister's parallel, that a faithful preacher speaks sometimes to the refreshment of others, the Gospel being a word in season to the weary, bread to the hungry and drink to the thirsty, even wine to them that are of a heavy heart, and most refreshing of all when the love of God is shed abroad in the heart through it and the presence of God enjoyed under it, and sometimes to the refreshment of himself with them; and whichever it be, he eases his mind and discharges his conscience when he truly declares the whole counsel of God. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the figure of the previous verse running: the skin-bottle, in which the wine was fermenting and ready to burst for want of vent, must be opened to be saved — 'I will open my mouth,' says Elihu, and so give the pent matter its escape.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the refreshment as more than mere relief of pressure. Elihu will speak not only that he may be eased of the pain of stifling his thoughts, but that he may have the pleasure of endeavouring, according to his place and capacity, to do good; for it is a great refreshment to a good man to have liberty to speak for the glory of God and the edification of others. Henry sets against it the grief of a good minister silenced and thrust into a corner, full of matter, full of Christ, full of heaven, and not suffered to speak of these things for the good of others. To have the liberty restored, then, is a double mercy — the easing of the speaker and the feeding of the hearers — and Elihu reaches for it as a man reaches for air.

So the verse completes the image of the wine-skin. What in the last verse threatened to burst is here given its vent; speech is not indulgence but release, and the young man opens his lips as a man opens a straining vessel, that the good matter within may flow out to profit rather than be lost in the bursting.
21:
Before he begins, Elihu binds himself in the words 'Let me not, I pray you, accept any man's person, neither let me give flattering titles unto man' to an impartiality that will flatter no side. The reformed John Gill spells out both temptations he renounces — neither the person of Job, for his poverty and affliction, indulging too much a pity that courts a good name, nor the persons of his three friends, for their wealth and grandeur; for neither the poor nor the rich are to be regarded in the deciding of a cause, but truth and justice only; the right of the matter is to be weighed without respect of persons. Elihu is resolved to respect no man's person, Gill says, and hopes Job and his friends will bear with him and excuse him for it. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the resolve as a pledge to speak the truth without fear or favour, and works out the phrase 'flattering titles': the word, from a root meaning to surname, is to put a fine name upon a man that does not belong to him, to beguile him by telling him he is what he is not. Titles of real office — ecclesiastical, civil, or military — are proper and never forbidden, since they serve for distinction; but the bombastic and sinfully complimentary titles of the East, by which the Arabs court their superiors, avoiding a man's proper name for some swelling epithet, are the thing Elihu will not stoop to. He will call no man by a name that is not his, nor beguile any with an epithet he has not earned.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the resolve into a rule of faithful speech. Elihu is determined to flatter no man, neither in compassion to Job, because he is poor and afflicted, making his case out better than it is for fear of increasing his grief, nor in compliment to the friends, because they are in prosperity and reputation; those in affliction must not be flattered but dealt faithfully with, and truth is not to be dissembled to court the favour of great men. Thou shalt not countenance a poor man in his cause any more than a rich, Henry says with the law of Exodus 23:3, nor regard a sad look any more than a big one, so as for its sake to pervert justice; for to be swayed by either is the very accepting of persons Elihu forswears. So the verse sets the terms of everything Elihu is about to say: he will weigh the persons of neither party, but speak, to poor and rich alike, only what he takes to be true.
22:
The chapter ends on the ground of Elihu's whole resolve, the fear of God that makes flattery impossible: 'For I know not to give flattering titles; in so doing my maker would soon take me away.' The reformed John Gill takes the confession plainly: Elihu had never been brought up to such language, nor used himself to it, nor could give such titles in conscience. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the second clause into a solemn self-warning: were he to flatter while under the influence he now feels, God might justly consume him in a moment; his Maker had made him to know truth, to tell truth, and to live by truth, and so, by God's help, he will speak the truth and nothing but the truth. Clarke gathers a wealth of examples of the swelling titles anciently heaped on worthless men, the flattering styles by which Eastern courts clothed their kings in the very attributes of the Deity — the sort of homage a man who feared his Maker could not render.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the same holy fear: the more closely we eye the majesty of God as our Maker, and the more we dread his wrath and justice, the less danger we are in of a sinful fearing or flattering of men; he that made us can take us away in his wrath, and will put lying and flattering lips to silence. John Wesley draws the identical moral in a line, that to eye God's majesty as our Maker is the surest cure of flattery.

Over the whole portrait of the young man the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the question the chapter leaves open: some commentators regard Elihu with great disfavour, as an empty and arrogant talker, chiefly from his swelling account of his own fulness; others accept him as a wise and pious friend who, more nearly than any other, hit the truth about Job's afflictions. Ellicott inclines to the kinder view, on the weighty ground that at the climax of the poem Elihu has no share in the condemnation God passes on the three friends, being noticed for neither praise nor blame; and he observes that these closing verses are a kind of soliloquy, unlike the address to the friends before and to Job after. So the chapter closes where the ancient Gregory had opened it — with the disputed estimate of a speaker who says much that is right, yet of whom it remains uncertain whether he speaks it with a right spirit or an overweening one.
